nameStory: The "scaly" in this lichen's name comes from the small, scale-like growths called phyllidia that dot its surface like tiny belly buttons. It's part of the "pelt" lichen family, named because these flat, leathery lichens were thought to resemble animal pelts spread out on the ground. The scientific name "praetextata" means "bordered" or "edged," referring to how these distinctive scales often line the lichen's margins.
description: Scaly pelt lichen is a leafy, flat lichen that spreads across the ground like a leathery mat. It's gray-green to brownish on top with a paler underside, and can grow several inches across. What makes this lichen special are the small, round, button-like growths called phyllidia scattered across its surface and edges. Like other pelt lichens, it feels somewhat like soft leather when dry and becomes more pliable when wet.

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Look for small, round, belly-button-like bumps called phyllidia scattered across the surface and especially along the edges - these feel slightly raised and firm to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms flat, leafy lobes that spread horizontally across the substrate like overlapping pieces of leather

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Gray-green to brownish on top when dry, becoming more vibrant green when wet; underside is typically pale or whitish

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Usually found growing on soil, moss, or among organic debris on the forest floor

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual lobes can reach 2-4 inches across, with the entire colony sometimes spanning 6 inches or more

habitat: Scaly pelt lichen thrives in moist, shaded areas throughout New England's forests, particularly in rich soil under deciduous and mixed woods. You'll often find it growing on humus-rich soil, over moss, or among leaf litter in areas that stay consistently damp. It prefers spots with good air quality away from pollution, making it more common in undisturbed forest areas.

seasonality.spring: Appears more vibrant green as spring moisture activates it. The phyllidia (button-like growths) are most noticeable when the lichen is hydrated from spring rains.
seasonality.summer: May look duller and more grayish during dry periods, but the distinctive phyllidia remain visible. Best observed after summer rains when it becomes pliable and colorful.
seasonality.fall: Often at its most visible as fallen leaves reveal it on the forest floor. The contrast between the pale underside and darker top surface is most apparent.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible under light snow cover. The leathery texture becomes more brittle in cold, dry conditions but the phyllidia are still identifiable.

funFact: The tiny button-like phyllidia on this lichen are actually miniature gardens - each one contains both the fungal and algal partners that make up the lichen, and they can break off to start entirely new lichen colonies, like biological seed packets scattered by wind or passing animals.
confusionNotes: Most other pelt lichens lack the distinctive phyllidia, making scaly pelt relatively easy to distinguish. The closest look-alike might be freckled pelt lichen, but that species has different markings (cephalodia that look more like freckles) and typically grows in different habitats. Remember: belly-button bumps = scaly pelt.
contextualKnowledge: The term "phyllidia" comes from Greek meaning "little leaves," though these structures look more like tiny buttons than leaves. These are actually specialized reproductive structures unique to certain lichen species - not all lichens have them, making this a particularly distinctive feature when present.
compareHints: Among the pelt lichens, scaly pelt is the only one in New England with prominent phyllidia scattered across its surface. Dog pelt lichen lacks these button-like growths entirely, while freckled pelt lichen has different spots called cephalodia that are flatter and more freckle-like rather than raised buttons. The phyllidia make scaly pelt one of the easier pelt lichens to identify with confidence.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the many pelt lichens in New England, horizontal pelt lichen is unique for its completely prostrate growth habit - it never curls up at the edges like dog pelt lichen or forms the ruffled, frilly margins of freckled pelt lichen.
Distinguished from dog pelt lichen by having many more fruiting structures along the edges rather than just a few large ones.

Among the many pelt lichens in New England, dog pelt lichen stands out for its preference for growing directly on soil rather than trees, and its particularly well-defined dark veining on a pale underside.
Among the pelt lichens, ruffled freckled pelt stands out for its notably bumpy, textured surface and strongly ruffled edges.
Unlike all other pelt lichens in New England, Eastern Waterfan is the only one that lives in water rather than on soil, rocks, or trees in terrestrial habitats.
Unlike the more common dog pelt lichen which has evenly-spaced, rounded lobes, alternating dog lichen has its distinctive alternating finger-like projections along the edges.
Among the pelt lichens, freckled pelt is the only one with distinctive dark green cephalodia (freckles), making identification fairly straightforward.
Unlike the common dog pelt lichen which has a smooth surface, peppered pelt is distinguished by its dark spotted pattern.
Among its pelt lichen relatives, sheepish pelt lichen is distinguished by its uniquely woolly surface texture - most other Peltigera species have smooth or slightly wrinkled surfaces.
Unlike the common dog pelt lichen which has a relatively uniform surface with veins on the underside, concentric pelt lichen displays obvious ring patterns on top.
Among the many pelt lichens in New England, field dog lichen stands out for its incredibly soft, velvety surface texture - most other dog lichens feel smoother or more leathery.
Carpet pelt lichen differs from its pelt lichen relatives by its consistently smooth upper surface and preference for soil rather than rocks or trees.

Among the many pelt lichen species in New England, membranous pelt lichen stands out for its distinctly thin, papery texture - much more delicate than the thicker, more leathery dog pelt lichen or scaly pelt lichen.
Unlike the smooth-surfaced dog pelt lichen or the powdery-edged freckled pelt lichen, mother-of-many pelt is immediately recognizable by its bumpy, phyllidia-covered surface.

Unlike the more common dog pelt lichen which has rounded, disk-like apothecia along the lobe edges, blacksaddle pelt has distinctive tubular, saddle-shaped reproductive structures on the lichen surface.

Compared to its Peltigera relatives, tree pelt lichen has a distinctly more velvety surface texture and tends to be more brownish in color than the grayer dog pelt lichen or the more distinctly veined fan pelt lichen.
Among its pelt lichen relatives, fan pelt lichen stands out with its smooth upper surface and distinctive raised black veins underneath.

Among pelt lichens, the pale-bellied pelt is distinguished by its consistently pale underside, whereas dog pelt lichen has a darker, often brownish underside with prominent veins, and freckled pelt lichen has distinctive dark spots on its upper surface.
